Figure 6. The continuous-integration matrix declared in the workflow: four jobs, each installing the package and its declared dependencies from scratch, running R CMD check –as-cran, the linter and — on one job only — the coverage report. The bar heights are typical wall-clock times for a package of this size rather than measurements; fail-fast: false keeps the other three running when one fails, which is what makes the matrix diagnostic rather than merely binary.

Three details in that YAML carry most of its value. setup-r-dependencies installs what DESCRIPTION declares, so a missing entry in Imports: fails the build rather than hiding behind the author’s library. error-on: '"warning"' turns an R CMD check warning — an undocumented argument, an undeclared dependency, a non-portable file name — into a failed build instead of a line nobody reads. And running on pull requests means a reviewer sees a green tick before reading a line, which changes the conversation from “does it work” to “is it right”. Journals increasingly check the same things the workflow does, and the journals whose policies require working code are measurably the ones whose papers can be rerun[14]. Pinning the environment itself — a renv.lock, a conda specification or a container built from it — is what makes the clean machine reproducible rather than merely clean[32][13].

11. Versions, NEWS and citation

A package that other work depends on needs a version number that means something. Semantic versioning encodes compatibility in three integers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a patch fixes a bug without changing behaviour, a minor release adds functionality compatibly, and a major release breaks something. For research software there is a fourth rule the group adds: a change that alters published numbers is a major release even if the interface is unchanged — the 0.3.0 entry in this package’s NEWS.md would have been 1.0.0 under that rule had the package been stable.

news <- readLines(file.path(PKG, "NEWS.md"))
heads <- grep("^# rockcurate", news, value = TRUE)
rel <- data.frame(version = sub("^# rockcurate ([0-9.]+).*$", "\\1", heads),
                  date = sub("^.*\\(([0-9-]+)\\).*$", "\\1", heads))
grp <- cumsum(grepl("^# rockcurate", news))
bodies <- split(news, grp)[as.character(seq_len(max(grp)))]   ## one block per release heading
rel$breaking <- vapply(bodies, function(b) any(grepl("Breaking", b)), logical(1))
rel$kinds <- vapply(bodies, function(b) {
  k <- unique(sub("^\\* \\*?\\*?([A-Za-z]+).*$", "\\1", grep("^\\* ", b, value = TRUE)))
  paste(k, collapse = ", ")}, character(1))
rel$x <- rev(seq_len(nrow(rel)))
print(ggplot(rel, aes(x, 0)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = breaking), size = 4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.22, label = paste0("v", version)), fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -0.22, label = date), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -0.42, label = kinds), size = 2.3, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = rel[rel$breaking, ], aes(y = 0.45, label = "changes published numbers"),
            size = 2.4, colour = "#b32d00") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = OKABE[1], `TRUE` = OKABE[2])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.6, 0.62)) + theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Release history read from NEWS.md") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9)))

print(rel[, c("version", "date", "breaking", "kinds")], row.names = FALSE)
##  version       date breaking           kinds
##    1.0.0 2026-10-18    FALSE   First, Golden
##    0.3.0 2026-09-30     TRUE Breaking, Fixed
##    0.2.0 2026-09-12    FALSE           Added
cat("\ncitation('rockcurate') reads inst/CITATION and prints:\n")
## 
## citation('rockcurate') reads inst/CITATION and prints:
print(utils::citation("rockcurate", lib.loc = LIB))
## To cite package 'rockcurate' in publications use:
## 
##   Bustos D (2026). _rockcurate: Curation of ChEMBL Bioactivity Tables_.
##   R package version 1.0.0,
##   <https://github.com/%3Corganisation%3E/rockcurate>.
## 
## A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is
## 
##   @Manual{,
##     title = {rockcurate: Curation of ChEMBL Bioactivity Tables},
##     author = {Daniel Bustos},
##     year = {2026},
##     note = {R package version 1.0.0},
##     url = {https://github.com/<organisation>/rockcurate},
##   }

Figure 7. The release history, parsed from the package’s own NEWS.md. The orange release is the one that changed scientific output — the aggregation rule — and is flagged as such, because a paper that used version 0.2.0 and a paper that used version 0.3.0 report different numbers from the same raw data. A version number in a Methods section is only useful if the NEWS file says what changed.

R packages carry their citation in two places, and the package written here has both. inst/CITATION is read by citation("rockcurate"), which is the command every R user already knows and the one that produces the BibTeX entry printed above. CITATION.cff is the ecosystem-neutral file that GitHub renders as a “Cite this repository” button and that Zenodo reads when archiving a release[5][6]. Software citation matters for two reasons: it is the only credit a methods developer receives, and it pins the exact version a result depends on. The group’s rule is that a paper cites the software it used with its version, and that the group’s own software carries both citation files and an archived DOI from the first release that produced a published number.

The licence decision is equally mechanical. Code goes out under MIT unless a dependency requires otherwise; data derived from ChEMBL keeps CC BY-SA 3.0, which propagates to derived tables; and a repository with no licence is, legally, a repository nobody may reuse — the default is “all rights reserved”, not “public domain”. R enforces part of this: R CMD check warns about a License: field it does not recognise, and CRAN refuses the package. Taken together, a versioned repository with a licence, a citation file, a NEWS file and an archived release is what the FAIR principles for research software ask for[7], and it is also the minimum that makes a project open to contributions from outside the group rather than readable only[8].

12. Documentation in four layers

Documentation fails when it is treated as one thing. It is four, each answering a different question and each with a different audience and lifetime[19][20]. In R the four map onto artefacts the tooling already knows about: README.md, the roxygen help pages, a vignette, and a pkgdown reference site generated from the first three.

exported <- getNamespaceExports("rockcurate")
rd_files <- sub("\\.Rd$", "", list.files(file.path(PKG, "man")))
docs <- data.frame(
  layer = c("README.md", "roxygen help pages", "vignette", "reference site"),
  question = c("Why does this exist and how do I run it in five minutes?",
               "What does this function do, what does it take and return?",
               "How do I do the thing I came for, end to end?",
               "What is the complete surface of the package?"),
  audience = c("a new user, or you in six months", "someone calling the function",
               "a student starting a project", "an advanced user; generated"),
  size = c(length(unlist(strsplit(readLines(file.path(PKG, "README.md")), "\\s+"))),
           length(rd_files), 0L, length(exported)))
kable(docs, col.names = c("layer", "question it answers", "audience", "size (words / count)"))
layer question it answers audience size (words / count)
README.md Why does this exist and how do I run it in five minutes? a new user, or you in six months 175
roxygen help pages What does this function do, what does it take and return? someone calling the function 18
vignette How do I do the thing I came for, end to end? a student starting a project 0
reference site What is the complete surface of the package? an advanced user; generated 15 
per_file <- data.frame(file = names(defs),
                       objects = vapply(defs, function(x) length(x$names), integer(1)))
per_file$documented <- vapply(names(defs), function(f)
  sum(defs[[f]]$names %in% rd_files | vapply(defs[[f]]$names, function(n)
    any(grepl(paste0("^", n, "$"), rd_files)), logical(1))), integer(1))
per_file$exported <- vapply(names(defs), function(f) sum(defs[[f]]$names %in% exported), integer(1))
long <- rbind(data.frame(file = per_file$file, what = "top-level objects", n = per_file$objects),
              data.frame(file = per_file$file, what = "exported", n = per_file$exported),
              data.frame(file = per_file$file, what = "with a help page", n = per_file$documented))
print(ggplot(long, aes(file, n, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("top-level objects" = "grey70", "exported" = OKABE[1],
                               "with a help page" = OKABE[3])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "count", fill = NULL, title = "Documentation coverage by file"))

cat(sprintf("%d exported objects, %d help pages, %d vignettes (the vignette is the layer this\n",
            length(exported), length(rd_files), 0))
## 15 exported objects, 18 help pages, 0 vignettes (the vignette is the layer this
cat("package is missing, and the one a new student would read first)\n")
## package is missing, and the one a new student would read first)

Figure 8. Top-level objects, exported objects and generated help pages per file. Every exported object has a help page, because roxygen2 generated one from the comment block beside it and R CMD check would fail otherwise; the internal objects deliberately have none. The missing layer is the vignette, which is the honest state of a package of this age: a README and complete help pages, no end-to-end narrative yet.

A README that takes five minutes to read is worth more than a reference site nobody generates. The order of effort is: README first, then roxygen blocks on the exported functions with at least one runnable @examples line each (R runs them during R CMD check, so an example that breaks is a failed build — documentation that is tested), then a vignette that solves one real task end to end, and only then a pkgdown site if the package has enough surface to need one.

13. Reviewing code, and being reviewed

Code review in a laboratory is not quality control by a superior; it is two people making sure that a piece of work can be defended. Industrial studies of review practice find that its measured value lies less in defect detection than in knowledge transfer and in the readability of what survives[22][23] — which is precisely what a research group needs when a student leaves.

review <- data.frame(
  area = c("Correctness", "Correctness", "Correctness", "Scientific validity", "Scientific validity",
           "Readability", "Readability", "Structure", "Structure", "Hygiene", "Reproducibility"),
  question = c("Does a test cover the behaviour that changed? Does the golden test still pass?",
               "Are floating-point comparisons made with a stated tolerance?",
               "Are edge cases handled: empty input, all values censored, a single compound?",
               "Is the change to the protocol recorded in NEWS.md and in the Methods?",
               "Do the defaults still reproduce the published reference table?",
               "Can the function be understood without reading its callers? Is the name honest?",
               "Is there a roxygen block saying what it takes, returns and errors on?",
               "Is I/O at the edges? Does the call graph stay acyclic?",
               "Are magic numbers in the configuration rather than in the expressions?",
               "Does the static check pass? Any leftover print(), commented-out code or large files?",
               "Are seeds fixed and dependencies declared where the result depends on them?"))
kable(review, col.names = c("area", "question the reviewer asks"))
area question the reviewer asks
Correctness Does a test cover the behaviour that changed? Does the golden test still pass?
Correctness Are floating-point comparisons made with a stated tolerance?
Correctness Are edge cases handled: empty input, all values censored, a single compound?
Scientific validity Is the change to the protocol recorded in NEWS.md and in the Methods?
Scientific validity Do the defaults still reproduce the published reference table?
Readability Can the function be understood without reading its callers? Is the name honest?
Readability Is there a roxygen block saying what it takes, returns and errors on?
Structure Is I/O at the edges? Does the call graph stay acyclic?
Structure Are magic numbers in the configuration rather than in the expressions?
Hygiene Does the static check pass? Any leftover print(), commented-out code or large files?

cat(sprintf("\n%d items; the first five are the ones worth a conversation, the rest should have been\n",
            nrow(review)))
## 
## 11 items; the first five are the ones worth a conversation, the rest should have been
cat("caught by the static check or the tests before the pull request was opened\n")
## caught by the static check or the tests before the pull request was opened

The etiquette matters as much as the checklist. Review the code, not the author: “this function reads the file twice” rather than “you did not think about efficiency”. Distinguish a blocking objection from a preference, and say which it is — the convention is to prefix non-blocking remarks with “nit:”. Ask questions when you do not understand instead of assuming an error. Approve when the change is an improvement, not when it is perfect; a review that demands perfection stops work. And on the receiving side: a review comment is information about your code, not about you, and the correct response to a good catch is to say so and fix it.

Bridge

The protocol packaged here was developed in Unit 6 and its raw data described in Unit 3; the reproducibility practices around it — version control, environments, provenance — are Unit 2, and the tabular idioms used throughout are Unit 4. The numbers this package produces are reported following Unit 23, scaled to a cluster and wrapped in a workflow manager in Unit 25, and served to collaborators as an application in Unit 26; the capstone, U27, expects the project to be delivered as a package of this shape. In the sister courses, Data curation develops the chemistry of the standardisation steps whose output is injected here, Standardisation explains why the largest-fragment and uncharging operations are ordered as they are, and the bioinformatics course’s Sequence alignment unit provides a second kind of pipeline — command-line tools glued together — on which the same packaging discipline applies. The Python edition of this unit, which builds the same protocol as a Python package with pytest and ruff, is here.

14. Summary

A notebook is a bench, a package is an instrument. The conversion is mechanical: pure functions for the computation, I/O at the edges, parameters in a checked configuration object, a thin Rscript entry point, and a DESCRIPTION that makes the whole thing installable[1][2].

Refactoring is only safe with a reference. The function extracted in Section 2 reproduced the laboratory’s curated table to within the precision of the stored file, and that comparison became the regression test that guards every later change.

Four layers of tests, each catching what the others cannot. Unit tests against hand-computed answers, tabulated tests over edge cases, property tests for invariants such as idempotence, and golden-file regression tests for the pipeline as a whole[21]. The injected one-line bug of Section 8 passed the configuration, structure and command-line tests and was caught only by the hand-worked aggregation test and the golden file — after changing the reported potency of about one per cent of the compounds by a median of half a log unit.

Coverage is a diagnostic, not a target. Read the uncovered objects; a suite can reach any percentage while asserting nothing.

Automate the arguments away. lintr, styler and pre-commit remove style from review; a four-job R-CMD-check matrix removes “works on my machine”; error-on: warning removes the slow erosion of the checks.

Make the software citable and the changes legible. Semantic versioning with a research-specific rule — anything that changes published numbers is a breaking change — a NEWS.md that says what changed, a licence, inst/CITATION and CITATION.cff[5][6].

Review is knowledge transfer. The checklist finds defects; the conversation is what keeps a pipeline usable after its author has graduated[22].

15. Self-assessment

  1. Why does an R package put its code in R/ and its documentation in man/ instead of keeping everything in one script?

Because the directory layout is a contract that the tooling enforces. R CMD INSTALL knows where to find the code, R CMD check can pair every exported object with its help page and fail when one is missing, roxygen2 can regenerate man/ and NAMESPACE from the comments beside the code, and the user gets ?curate for free. A script offers none of these, which is why a script cannot be checked.

  1. What makes a function “pure”, and why does purity make testing cheap? What does data.table do to purity?

Its result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself: no global state, no file reads, no side effects. Such a function is tested by calling it and comparing the return value — no fixtures, no temporary files, no ordering between tests. data.table’s := modifies its argument in place, so a function using it silently changes the caller’s object; the package therefore calls data.table::copy() before modifying, which is why harmonise_units() can be called twice with the same answer.

  1. Give the hand-worked aggregation example and the number the buggy version would produce.

Compound A has measurements 7.0 and 7.4 (exact) and 6.2 (censored). The protocol takes the median of the exact values, 7.20. The reverted rule takes the median of all three, 7.0. The difference is 0.2 log units for that compound, and across the real data set the bug changed the potency of about one per cent of the compounds by a median of half a log unit, with a tail several times the experimental error, moving compounds across the potency threshold used for classification.

  1. A colleague says their suite has 100 % coverage, so the code is correct. Respond.

Coverage measures which code ran, not whether anything was checked. A suite that calls every function and asserts nothing reaches 100 %. Conversely, the objects not exercised in Section 7 are a short, inspectable list, and for each one the question is “missing test or acceptable gap?”. Coverage is useful read item by item and misleading as a single number to maximise.

  1. Which kind of test would have caught a change in the unit-conversion table, and which would not?

The tabulated test asserting that 1 nM gives pActivity 9 and 1,000 nM gives 6 catches it immediately. The golden-file test catches it too, but only reports that the whole pipeline moved. Property tests do not: idempotence and determinism hold for the wrong conversion as well. This is why the suite has layers — the unit test localises, the golden test guarantees.

  1. Why did the buggy package have to be installed into a second library and tested in a separate process?

Because rockcurate was already attached in this session, and R caches a namespace once it is loaded: editing the file, or even reinstalling the package over itself, does not change the functions the running session will call. A second library plus a child process started by callr gives an unambiguous answer. The same reasoning applies to any “I fixed it” claim made without restarting the session.

  1. What belongs in a configuration file, and what belongs in the code?

Values a user may legitimately change for their project — the organism, the heavy-atom window, the plausibility bounds — belong in configuration, with defaults in the code that reproduce the published protocol. The structure of the protocol itself, the order of the filters and the aggregation rule do not: making them configurable would turn a reproducible protocol into a family of protocols with no name. The test “the defaults are the published protocol” is what prevents the defaults from drifting.

  1. Under the group’s versioning rule, what version follows 1.4.2 after a fix that changes the curated output by 0.05 log units?

2.0.0. The interface did not change, so semantic versioning in its usual reading would suggest 1.4.3, but any change that alters published numbers is treated as breaking: papers citing 1.4.2 and 2.0.0 report different results from the same input, and a reader must be able to see that from the version alone. The NEWS entry must say which numbers moved and by how much.

  1. What does a “software availability” statement commit the group to?

That a repository exists at the stated address, that it contains the code that produced the published numbers (tagged or archived at a DOI, not just the current main branch), that it declares its dependencies and licence, and that it runs somewhere other than the author’s laptop — which is what the R-CMD-check matrix demonstrates. Anything less turns the statement into a claim the group cannot support.

  1. Write three review comments on a pull request that adds a new filter to the protocol, in the group’s style.

“Blocking: this filter changes the compound count, so the golden test needs updating and NEWS.md needs a breaking-change entry — can you add both?”; “Could you move the 0.35 similarity cut-off into curation_config()? It is the kind of number a reviewer will ask about and it should have one definition.”; “nit: f is hard to search for; filter_by_similarity would be easier to find in six months.” The first is blocking and scientific, the second structural, the third a preference marked as such.

  1. Your package draws a figure as a side effect inside a computation function. Why is that a design error, and what is the fix?

Because it mixes a pure computation with an output action: the function cannot be called in a loop, on a cluster or inside a test without opening a device or writing files, and its result can no longer be compared with an expected value. The fix is to return the numbers and let a separate plotting function — or the document — draw them. The same argument applies to functions that print() instead of returning, and to functions that use message() for results rather than for progress.

  1. A language model wrote a plausible implementation of a new aggregation rule. What do you do before merging it?

Read it, then make it earn its place in the suite: add a hand-worked unit test for the new rule, check that the existing golden test either still passes or fails for a reason you can explain, run the static checks, and record the behavioural change in NEWS.md with a version bump. The tests are the contract; whether a human or a model wrote the code changes nothing about what must be demonstrated before it is trusted.

Glossary

Continuous integration (CI)
Automatic execution of R CMD check and the test suite on a clean machine on every push, across a matrix of operating systems and R versions.
Coverage
The fraction of code executed while the tests run; measured per line by covr and, here, per exported object by tracing the namespace. A diagnostic listing untested code, not a quality score.
DESCRIPTION
The metadata file that makes a directory an R package: name, version, licence, and the declared Imports and Suggests.
Fixture
A helper that builds the objects a test needs — in testthat, a function defined in a helper-*.R file, loaded automatically before the tests.
Golden-file (regression) test
A test comparing the output of a pipeline with a stored, reviewed reference; the guard that makes refactoring safe.
Idempotence
The property that applying an operation twice gives the same result as applying it once; here, re-aggregating an already aggregated table.
NAMESPACE
The generated file declaring which objects a package exports and which S3 methods it registers.
Pre-commit hook
A check that runs automatically before a commit is created, keeping failing code out of the history.
Property test
A test asserting an invariant that must hold for every input, rather than a specific output for a specific input.
Pure function
A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing outside itself.
roxygen2
The package that turns #’ comment blocks beside the code into man/*.Rd help pages and into NAMESPACE.
S3 class
R’s lightest object system: an attribute naming the class, plus methods called generic.class; used here for the configuration and the log.
Semantic versioning
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering encoding compatibility; in this group extended so that any change to published numbers is a major release.
testthat
R’s standard testing framework: test_that() blocks of expect_*() assertions, run by file, with helpers loaded automatically. 
detach("package:rockcurate", unload = TRUE)
for (path in c(PKG, BUG, LIB, BUGLIB, file.path(TMP, "out"))) unlink(path, recursive = TRUE)
Sys.unsetenv(c("ROCKCURATE_RAW", "ROCKCURATE_REF", "ROCKCURATE_SCRIPT", "ROCKCURATE_LIB"))
cat("package sources removed:", !dir.exists(PKG), !dir.exists(BUG), "\n")
## package sources removed: TRUE TRUE
cat("temporary libraries removed:", !dir.exists(LIB), !dir.exists(BUGLIB), "\n")
## temporary libraries removed: TRUE TRUE
cat("rockcurate still attached:", "package:rockcurate" %in% search(), "\n")
## rockcurate still attached: FALSE

Nothing a document writes outside its own outputs should survive it. In a real project the package is a repository of its own, the document that uses it only calls library(rockcurate), and the only thing the analysis keeps is the version number — which it records in the Methods, as Unit 23 required.
